How on Earth did you reach that conclusion? A trivial look at that list:
* Web browsers. -- Worked so well that IE remained the dominant browser for over a decade [1]. Of course, bundling was important here too but without the intentional incompatibilities between IE and Netscape, bundling alone would not have been nearly as effective.
* Office documents. -- Despite .docx files being notionally based on an open standard, to this day, Microsoft office will frequently reject as "corrupted" .docx files that have been edited using other implementations of the OOXML standard (in my experience, particularly when tracked changes are enabled or images are involved). In most such cases in my experience, the sentiment from coworkers is "why don't you just install Word" --- so apparently still working as intended.
* Instant messaging -- seems to have worked pretty well at the time [2] and remained popular for nearly a decade. And while they later lost marketshare to transformationally different technologies (texting, mobile messaging), the competitors against which they used the strategy remain dead.
* Against Java -- Led to major legal action, in which Microsoft was forced to pay Sun >$2B and agree to discontinue the practice in settlements, presumably only because by now people were catching on to the strategy. Failing that, Microsoft just made a separate competing language for cross-platform (AKA "write once run anywhere" :) development and called it....     .NET [3]
> And it's strictly better than Microsoft spending their time enhancing closed-source software, no? That was my question at the end: they could make .NET closed-source
Presumably it is reasonable to assume that they would like to grow the market share of .NET. While more open code is usually good, I would indeed not consider it "strictly better" if their goal in this work is to capture market share against other languages by leveraging the popularity and community that comes with "Open Source", while leaving them in a position where they can then reassert hegemonic control over their language via exactly the pathway being discussed here.

That seems unsurprising, right? Probably all physics we experience - light-surface interactions, surfaces at the atomic scale, and waves in air and water - are all made entirely of only small perturbations, but enough of them the result is statistically stable.
The popular idea of the butterfly effect in weather has always seemed suspect to me, due to the fact that air is a naturally damped system; a butterfly’s influence on air drops over distance, and likely falls off fast enough that the probability it can affect something even a few miles away is below atomic or quantum thresholds. The analogy between weather and simple mathematical chaotic systems seems specious.
Looking around a little it seems like some physicists are starting to agree, and believe Lorenz’ observations based on his weather modeling has more to do with the modeling and limited numerics than reality: “the limited predictability within the Lorenz 1969 model is explained by scale interactions in one article[22] and by system ill-conditioning in another more recent study.[25]” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly_effect#Recent_debate...

storyTitle: Space Garbage Solutions Could Help Fix Earth’s Plastic Problem
text:
In the spirit of “Don’t saying anything if you can’t say something nice” – All I can say about this article is – It is great that people are looking in to solutions for ocean plastics  including this sort of article. Sometimes hard problems are solved by someone asking ‘why don’t we solve xyz by doing abc?’. I had hopes that this might be one of the occasions but after reading the article I sadly doubt that this is one of those times.
The difference is that things in space have an orbit that is calculable (be that in synchronous or decaying orbits). In other words, if you missed it this time round, it will be in position B on the next orbit.  Things drifting on the ocean currents? You get one and only one opportunity to pick up and collect it (unless you pick up your sooper-dooper-plastic-scooper and move it). Actually, thinking about it that more or less equates to a space-sooper-dooper-scooper missing it on the first pass and having to expend fuel to go up or down to catch it on the next go-round. In other words, I’ve painted myself in to a corner and it is a 1-1 in terms of practicality (or 0-0 for the pragmatists) .
My next thought was – Sheesh – how wide would the net/catcher/sooper-dooper-scooper have to be to catch debris in space versus on the ocean. That lead to some fascinating internet research on exactly how precise GEO satellites are these days (in terms of is a 0.5/1/5/10/20/100/1000 mile variance ok?) In other words – how wide of a corridor would your sooper-dooper-space-scooper have to be in order to be effective versus how wide your sooper-dooper-ocean-scooper would have to be. Needless to say, answers varied from the “we don’t talk about fight-club” through to Wikipedia levels. Best answer I can provide is to DDG how precise GPS satellites need to be and then scale it to the earths’ circumference.  Maths is hard, especially space maths but to save you the pain - I painted myself in to a corner again.
Current score 2-2 (or 0-0).
Next, on to using machine vision to identify and target. Here there is a clear victor. Consider the difficulty of the following – Detecting any object that shouldn’t be there (in space) versus detecting ‘something that glitters/differs from the background sea color’. Is it a fish? The sun glinting on the waves? A bit of plastic? Have to give a goal to the space sooper-dooper-scooper here.
Current score 2-3 (or 0-1).
Now on to the thing that I really wanted to touch on.Chaos theory. Yum. Specifically the Butterfly effect ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly_effect ) As mentioned earlier, orbits are calculable. A single piece of plastic drifting on the ocean affected by winds, tides, passing ships, storms, a dolphin playing tag with it etc etc etc?) That right there is supercomputer level hard type math with a (charitable) less than 100% degree of certainty (think weather forecasts and the computing power used to calculate the probability and paths of major events like tornados). Those are a lot bigger than a floating rubber duck (28,000 Rubber Ducks Accidentally Fell Into The Sea In 1992
https://www.ranker.com/list/rubber-ducks-friendly-floatees-o... )
Current score 2-4 (or 0-2).
Now, on to the thing that makes me think that the problems of space debris are easier to solve that the problems of plastics in the ocean. I remembered reading something from a few years back that more or less was about an island of garbage floating in the North Pacific. Searching for references turned up some debunking (which was a shame since I wanted to make the point of “if we haven’t hoovered up the ocean plastics neatly gathered in a neat bundle for us then why haven’t we done it yet?) (ref The Truth About the Great Pacific Garbage Patch http://factmyth.com/factoids/there-is-a-plastic-garbage-isla...)
Current score 2-4 (or 0-2).
Wow. You made it this far? I’m amazed and will try to trim down some of the wall of text.
Here is the TLDR; Space sooper-dooper-scooper advantages? Harvesting solar energy to blast a stream of ionized particles to blow space debris down further versus the butterfly effect.  Ever seen those industrial machines that use a blast of precisely timed air to blow defective products off to one side? Then you have a rough idea of the concept.
Current score 2-5 (or 0-3).
The only transferable technology might possibly be the ‘Sticky Net’ concept https://www.surrey.ac.uk/surrey-space-centre/missions/remove... . There is some research on an unrelated field that uses synthetic spider silk (versus the toxic to marine life formulation) space spray foam approach.
The biggest problem with that is that in a space orbit – anything that shouldn’t be there can be considered ‘garbage’ and for removal. Doing that in the ocean where the ‘thing’ could be a fish, a jelly-fish or a piece of plastic?  Way too much risk of collateral damage.
Certainly food for thought although I make the final score in terms of practicality 2-6 (or 0-5). There needs to be a solutions to ocean plastics but this ain’t it.
Armchair Quaterback aka Personal opinion only.
[Edit to add] I overlooked the elephant in the room. Monitoring who throws what, where and when in to space is a solved problem so it is a 'clean once and done' type task. Tracking who threw that plastic bag in the ocean and when/where? Not possible.

text:
The Fourth Amendment prohibits "unreasonable searches and seizures," which the Supreme Court has broadly interpreted to include things such as warrantless wiretaps [1] and even certain types of cell phone call metadata [2]. Effectively, if a person expects their conversations to be private, and society views these as reasonably private (e.g. not taking place in the open, where anyone could overhear), warrantless covert government access constitutes unreasonable search and violates constitutional rights. To quote Supreme Court Justice John Marshall II:
"My understanding of the rule that has emerged from prior decisions is that there is a twofold requirement, first that a person have exhibited an actual (subjective) expectation of privacy and, second, that the expectation be one that society is prepared to recognized as "reasonable." Thus a man's home is, for most purposes, a place where he expects privacy, but objects, activities, or statements that he exposes to the "plain view" of outsiders are not "protected" because no intention to keep them to himself has been exhibited. On the other hand, conversations in the open would not be protected against being overheard, for the expectation of privacy under the circumstances would be unreasonable."
Note that this statement was in agreement to a court decision saying that government wiretapping of a public phone booth was unconstitutional, because when you're in a phone booth with the door closed, you don't expect people to overhear you, and thus it's an unreasonable search and a violation of constitutional rights for the government to record your conversation. Note that this doesn't depend on notions of "trespass" or specific areas, and rather depends on a person's expectation of privacy:
"For the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places. What a person knowingly exposes to the public, even in his own home or office, is not a subject of Fourth Amendment protection. But what he seeks to preserve as private, even in an area accessible to the public, may be constitutionally protected."
OP is almost certainly correct that dragnet, warrantless searching of private message data by the government is a violation of constitutional rights, although it'll take a Supreme Court case to make a real ruling on the subject.
[1] Katz v. the United States (1967) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katz_v._United_States
[2] Carpenter v. the United States (2018) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpenter_v._United_States

Wait, what? TAI is the one time standard that doesn't change. It's just a bunch of atomic clocks averaged together. As monotonic as human kind is able to manufacture, at this time.

The varying offset of UTC, called leap seconds, is what's annoying to computers. If we ran computers on TAI, they would be simpler!
